parsed.narrative: With the default choices, the religiosity-well-being relation grows with perceived cultural norms: interaction beta = 0.045 (95% CI 0.026 to 0.063), p < 0.001, n = 10,535, so the verdict is DEPENDS ON NORMS. Borges ran 15 universes: the baseline, 14 single changes and 0 combinations. 1 of 15 universes change the verdict (robustness 93%); the estimate runs from 0.018 to 0.046. The nearest verdict change takes a single change (fit the model: Pooled OLS, robust errors): interaction beta = 0.018 (95% CI -0.000 to 0.037), p = 0.056, n = 10,535. The estimate stays positive; it is the p-value that crosses 0.05. Re-running it in a fresh sandbox reproduced the same numbers. The 105 research teams that reported a standardised effect range from -0.045 to 0.282 (median 0.039), and 68 of them (65%) have an interval above zero.
caveats: The share of universes that agree is a property of the explored set, which is built from the choices the teams documented and searched for flips; it is not a population estimate.
Standardised coefficients describe an association in a convenience sample of 24 countries; they do not show that religion causes well-being.
